responseBinding.questionText: The area over which the wind collects loose snow is the ______.

rows.sourceExcerpt: Design begins upwind. The fetch is the distance over which wind can gather loose snow before it reaches the fence. responseBinding.questionText: The passage describes the deliberately porous structure as a ______.

rows.sourceExcerpt: A snow fence works by changing wind flow, not by acting as a solid wall. The barrier is deliberately porous. responseBinding.questionText: The author believes algorithms remove moral choices from disaster triage.

rows.sourceExcerpt: After a disaster, needs arrive faster than agencies can inspect them. Roads may be blocked, communications intermittent and records incomplete. Triage is unavoidable: someone must decide which request receives attention first. Algorithms can support prioritisation by combining reports, location and available resources. Their attraction is not that they remove values but that they apply a stated rule quickly across many cases. The danger begins when speed is mistaken for certainty or when the rule’s moral choices are hidden inside technical language.

Ambos tratan «remove», pero la proposición añade «algorithms», «moral», «choices», «disaster», «triage» donde la fuente especifica «attraction», «values», «apply», «rule», «quickly», «across». Esa diferencia verificable niega la relación formulada y justifica NO.

responseBinding.questionText: Areas with poor communications may appear less needy than they really are.

rows.sourceExcerpt: A model can rank only what enters its data. Neighbourhoods with reliable connections may submit more detailed reports than equally affected areas that are offline. If report volume is treated as need, visibility becomes advantage. Missing reports are not evidence of safety. Designers can introduce uncertainty flags or seek alternative signals, but no adjustment fully replaces local knowledge. The output should therefore be read as a provisional map of recorded information, not as a complete picture of suffering.

responseBinding.questionText: Every reasonable objective produces the same order of requests.

rows.sourceExcerpt: Different objectives produce different queues. Minimising travel time may favour clusters of accessible requests; reducing the greatest immediate risk may send teams farther apart; supporting the largest number of people may disadvantage a small isolated community. None of these calculations is neutral. A priority rule expresses what counts as benefit and whose delay is acceptable. responseBinding.questionText: Which best expresses the author’s conclusion?
responseBinding.correctOptionText: Algorithms can assist, but institutions remain responsible for their design and use

rows.sourceExcerpt: The sensible position is neither automatic trust nor blanket rejection. Algorithmic triage can organise information and expose a consistent priority rule, but responsibility remains institutional. Agencies choose objectives, collect data, set override powers and decide how uncertainty is communicated. A model that accelerates a bad rule is not an improvement. A carefully governed tool, by contrast, can help staff see a crowded situation without pretending to replace judgement. The relevant question is not whether an algorithm decides, but how people design, supervise and answer for its role.

responseBinding.questionText: Customer surname: ______

bindings.audiblePhrase: It is Pritchlow, P-R-I-T-C-H-L-O-W, not Pritchard as the earlier enquiry suggested. Please use the longer spelling on the collection record.

responseBinding.questionText: Rug material: ______

bindings.audiblePhrase: The pile is wool, natural sheep wool. The fringe may contain cotton, but the main rug material you should record is wool.

responseBinding.questionText: Main stain: ______

bindings.audiblePhrase: There is a small pet mark by the door, but the main visible stain is coffee in the centre. One fringe corner is loose as well.

responseBinding.questionText: Approximate width: ______ metres

bindings.audiblePhrase: It is about three metres long and 2.1 metres wide. The 2.1 figure is the approximate width for the form.

responseBinding.questionText: Collection date: ______

bindings.audiblePhrase: Yes, 12 January is suitable. I will keep the afternoon free, and the rug can remain flat on the floor until the crew arrives.

responseBinding.questionText: Access note: use the ______ entrance

bindings.audiblePhrase: The front stair turns too sharply, so please use the courtyard entrance. The crew can carry the rug out flat through there.

responseBinding.questionText: Blue border

bindings.audiblePhrase: At the workshop, the first special step concerns the blue border. Because that colour may release dye, we carry out a colour test before any wet treatment.

responseBinding.questionText: General dust

bindings.audiblePhrase: For the general dust, the planned treatment is a controlled surface clean rather than soaking. Odour treatment is a separate option and has not been selected.

responseBinding.questionText: Coffee mark

bindings.audiblePhrase: The coffee mark is listed for spot treatment after the fibre and colour checks. We will contact you if the hidden test shows an unexpected reaction.

responseBinding.questionText: Flat drying

bindings.audiblePhrase: It will lie on a drying rack and dry flat; it will not hang. Once fully dry, it is wrapped for transport, never sealed while damp.

responseBinding.questionText: Load unexposed film

bindings.audiblePhrase: The completely light-tight film-loading bench is station A. That is where unexposed film is loaded into a processing tank.

responseBinding.questionText: Begin processing paper

bindings.audiblePhrase: Paper processing starts at the developer station, B. Keep the developer tongs there rather than carrying them to the wash sink.

responseBinding.questionText: Rinse finished prints

bindings.audiblePhrase: Finished prints receive their extended rinse in the wash sink, the sink reserved for washing, after the fixing stage is complete.

responseBinding.questionText: Collect labelled negatives

bindings.audiblePhrase: Labelled negative sleeves are returned through the negative cabinet, D. Loose strips must never be left on a table.

responseBinding.questionText: Dry fibre-based prints

bindings.audiblePhrase: Fibre-based prints that are ready for controlled drying go to the print dryer at E after members complete the separate demonstration.

responseBinding.questionText: Why must members book a full session?
responseBinding.correctOptionText: to prevent overlap at shared stations

bindings.audiblePhrase: Book a full session because the stations are shared and overlap creates unsafe crowding. The booking does not guarantee one-to-one teaching.

responseBinding.questionText: What should a member do if the safe light fails?
responseBinding.correctOptionText: cover materials and call the supervisor

bindings.audiblePhrase: If the safe light fails, do not use a phone. Cover light-sensitive materials immediately and call the supervisor from the doorway.

responseBinding.questionText: Where are personal chemicals kept?

bindings.audiblePhrase: Personal chemicals are accepted only in the checked storage locker, with contents and owner clearly labelled.

responseBinding.questionText: What is required before using the print dryer?

bindings.audiblePhrase: The print dryer becomes available after a dry-mounting demonstration. It does not require another card or a payment each time.

responseBinding.questionText: How are spills reported?

bindings.audiblePhrase: Tell the duty supervisor about every spill immediately. Do not hide the report in the calendar or write it only on an envelope.

responseBinding.questionText: Identify substances purchased by the workshop

bindings.audiblePhrase: The trade ledger lists materials the workshop actually purchased, so it can identify substances available even when no mixing instructions survive.

responseBinding.questionText: Show how a mixture was described

bindings.audiblePhrase: A recipe inventory gives the language and proportions used to describe a mixture, although we must not assume the workers followed it exactly.

responseBinding.questionText: Confirm residue on a surviving tool

bindings.audiblePhrase: A material sample taken from a surviving tool can confirm residue, but contamination and later conservation treatment have to be considered.

responseBinding.questionText: Record a remembered sensory impression

bindings.audiblePhrase: An oral history records a remembered sensory impression. It is valuable evidence of experience, not a chemical measurement.

responseBinding.questionText: Locate likely ventilation points

bindings.audiblePhrase: The building survey can locate doors, roof vents and other likely ventilation points, helping us understand how odour may have moved.

responseBinding.questionText: The exhibit will describe the result as an ______.

bindings.audiblePhrase: The label should call the recreated smell an interpretation, not the authentic smell of every workshop day.

responseBinding.questionText: Visitors will smell the mixture on a ______.

bindings.audiblePhrase: Visitors will not inhale from a bottle. A single-use scent strip gives a controlled optional encounter.

responseBinding.questionText: A screening question will identify fragrance ______.

bindings.audiblePhrase: Before participation, one screening question asks about fragrance sensitivity, without demanding private medical details.

responseBinding.questionText: The first trial will use a ______ concentration.

bindings.audiblePhrase: The first trial uses a low concentration. We can increase it only if detection is poor and the safety boundary still holds.

responseBinding.questionText: Responses will be recorded with an anonymous ______.

bindings.audiblePhrase: To separate feedback from names, each response sheet receives an anonymous code that links only to the session condition.

responseBinding.questionText: Dormant cells survive beneath the winter ______.

bindings.audiblePhrase: Many snow algae persist as dormant cells beneath the winter snow pack, the compact layer of seasonal snow, becoming active only when conditions improve.

responseBinding.questionText: Growth increases when liquid ______ becomes available.

bindings.audiblePhrase: Growth accelerates when liquid meltwater becomes available around the grains; cold alone does not mean the habitat is completely dry.

responseBinding.questionText: A protective ______ can colour the snow red.

bindings.audiblePhrase: Some cells produce a protective pigment that screens intense radiation and can make a snow surface appear red or pink.

responseBinding.questionText: Wind-blown ______ may supply nutrients.

bindings.audiblePhrase: Nutrients may arrive with wind-blown dust, but the amount and source differ among sites and storms.

responseBinding.questionText: Darker snow has lower surface ______.

bindings.audiblePhrase: When biological colour darkens the surface, its albedo—the fraction of incoming light reflected—can decrease.

responseBinding.questionText: More absorbed energy can accelerate ______.

bindings.audiblePhrase: Lower reflection means more energy is absorbed, which can accelerate snowmelt under suitable weather conditions.

responseBinding.questionText: Why do researchers sample several colour patches?
responseBinding.correctOptionText: to capture variation in the community

bindings.audiblePhrase: Researchers sample several colour patches because one red area does not represent the whole community; spatial variation is part of the result.

responseBinding.questionText: What is a limitation of satellite colour data?
responseBinding.correctOptionText: other materials can produce similar colours

bindings.audiblePhrase: Satellite colour covers large regions, but mineral dust and other materials can look similar, so colour alone does not uniquely identify algae.

responseBinding.questionText: What does the lecturer say about the feedback effect?

bindings.audiblePhrase: The feedback is plausible, yet its strength varies among sites. It should not be described as the dominant cause of melting everywhere.

responseBinding.questionText: Why are repeated measurements needed?
responseBinding.correctOptionText: to follow change through the melt season

bindings.audiblePhrase: Repeated measurements follow change through the melt season, separating a single snapshot from a developing biological and physical process.
